# Publishing That Rebuilds Itself {#sec-quarto}

```{python}
#| label: ch1-setup
from scripts.prose import number_words
# Which London outputs read the attraction counts? Count the formats of every page in the
# finished London project whose source reads data/attractions.csv.
from pathlib import Path

import yaml

ldn = Path("../examples/london")
readers = {}
for qmd in sorted(ldn.glob("*.qmd")):
    text = qmd.read_text()
    if "attractions.csv" not in text:
        continue
    fmt = yaml.safe_load(text.split("---")[1]).get("format", "html")
    readers[qmd.name] = len(fmt) if isinstance(fmt, dict) else 1
n_pages = len(readers)
n_outputs = sum(readers.values())

WORDS = number_words(zero="no")


def in_words(n: int) -> str:
    """Small counts as words in prose; larger ones as figures."""
    return WORDS.get(n, f"{n:,}")
```

An analyst runs a script and copies a number into a Word document. She pastes a chart into a
slide, retypes the number in an email and exports a PDF for the website. Four copies now exist,
and the script knows about none of them. Next month the data are revised. The script runs again
in a moment; the copies have to be found, one by one, and nobody can say whether the one in the
email was ever fixed. Nothing here was careless. Each copy was a small act of faith that the
number was right and would stay right, and most reports are still built this way: by hand, on
faith.

::: story
<!-- source: REVISION-PLAN.md line 474, WP3 ("roadmap alt text and Appendix I's agenda now
computed (they had typed chapter numbers already out of date)"); book/PLAN.md lines 607–608
(§15, item 5: the chapters renumbered, "the landing page and roadmaps follow from the
sources") -->
This book did it too. The descriptions of its part maps, which screen readers read aloud, and
the agenda in an appendix named chapters by typed numbers. The numbering moved; the typed numbers
did not, in a book about not typing numbers. A typed number is never an error to the program
that prints it. Both are computed from the chapter list now, and cannot fall behind it.
:::

The alternative is **one source that rebuilds every output**, the Publish step of this book's
loop. The more of that work a program does, the fewer places an error can slip in, and anyone
can see where each number came from and rebuild it. Readers get documents that agree with each
other and with the data.

::: opener
- Explain why numbers copied by hand drift out of date, and how one source that rebuilds
  every output prevents it.
- Trace a `.qmd` file through the three steps of `quarto render`, and say which step a given
  error comes from.
- Distinguish what Quarto does from what a coding agent does, and say how each is
  checked.
- Decide whether a document is worth building with Quarto, from what "reproducible" promises
  and where Quarto is the wrong tool.
:::

## Why reports drift {#sec-drift}

The London visitor guide that runs through Part II is a small example of a common problem.
The tourism office publishes the same facts to several audiences: a web guide for
visitors, a dashboard for managers, a Word brief for partners, a square social-media card
and, later, a white paper. In the finished project, `{python} in_words(n_pages)` pages read
the same table of attraction visits, counted by the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions
(ALVA), and between them they write `{python} in_words(n_outputs)` files: the guide alone
becomes a web page, a Word document, a PDF, a PowerPoint deck, an e-book and a slide deck that
runs in the browser.

Kept by hand, those `{python} in_words(n_outputs)` files would be
`{python} in_words(n_outputs)` copies of the same counts, and three things go wrong with
copies:

- **Stale numbers.** One copy is missed, and the partner brief disagrees with the dashboard.
- **Lost provenance.** Six months later, nobody can say which version of the data
  produced the number in the white paper.
- **Slow change.** Because every update is expensive, updates stop happening, and the
  documents quietly age.

The same three failures turn up wherever numbers are published more than once: the monthly
pack whose chart disagrees with its summary, the evaluation whose deck quotes last week's
score, the investor update that copies a figure from the wrong month. They are what happens
when the *output* is treated as the thing you edit. The fix is structural: edit the source,
and let a program rebuild the outputs. @fig-drift follows one correction from ALVA through
both workflows.

![By hand, copies go stale; from one source, one render updates them all.](../media/diagrams/drift){#fig-drift .on-light fig-alt="Two ways to publish the London guide's attraction counts after ALVA corrects one figure in attractions.csv. By hand: each number is copied into each output, one at a time, so the web guide and the dashboard get the new number while the Word brief, the social card and the white paper still show the old one. One source: code cells in the project's .qmd pages read attractions.csv, and one quarto render rebuilds the web guide, the dashboard, the Word brief, the social card and the white paper, all with the corrected number."}

## What Quarto is {#sec-what-quarto}

Quarto is an open-source publishing system, free for anyone to use: a *command-line
program*, one you run by typing a command in a terminal (@sec-step-terminal), that turns
plain-text source files into finished documents.

The input is either a plain Markdown file (`.md`) or a Quarto document (`.qmd`). *Markdown*
is a way of writing structured text with a few punctuation marks, such as `#` before a
heading (@sec-markdown). A `.qmd` file is Markdown with two additions: a block of settings at
the top, written in *YAML*, a format for settings in which indentation is meaning
(@sec-qmd-basics), and *code cells*, fenced blocks of code that run when the document is built.
Here is a complete one, the file the test run in @sec-setup asks your agent to write:

````markdown
---
title: "Hello"
format:
  html: default
  typst: default
---

```{{python}}
answer = 6 * 7
```

The answer is `{{python}} answer`.
````

Between the two `---` lines are the settings: a title and two formats, a web page (`html`)
and a PDF (`typst`). The fenced block below them is a code cell. The sentence
at the bottom contains *inline code*: when the document is built, Quarto runs `answer` and
writes its value into the sentence. When this book was built, the same
calculation gave `{python} 6 * 7`, and that number was computed, not typed.

### Three steps: execute, convert, typeset

To *render* a document is to build its outputs from its source, and `quarto render` does it
in three steps (@fig-pipeline).

1. **Execute.** Jupyter, a computation engine, runs the code cells. The results (numbers,
   tables, figures) replace the code in an intermediate Markdown file. The cells run once for
   each format, so each output gets results made for it (@sec-formats).
2. **Convert.** For each format, Pandoc, a long-established document converter, reads that
   Markdown and writes the output: HTML, Word (`docx`), EPUB, PowerPoint (`pptx`) or a
   Reveal.js slide deck.
3. **Typeset.** For PDF, Pandoc writes source for Typst, a modern typesetting system that
   ships inside Quarto, and Typst produces the PDF.

![What `quarto render` does. One source becomes Markdown with results, which Pandoc converts to each output format; for PDF, Typst typesets the result.](../media/diagrams/render-pipeline){#fig-pipeline .on-light fig-alt="A source file, london.qmd, holding Markdown, YAML and code cells, goes through three steps. Step 1, execute: Jupyter for Python or knitr for R runs each code cell. The result is Markdown with the results in place of the code. Step 2, convert: Pandoc turns that Markdown into html, docx, epub, pptx and revealjs. Step 3, typeset: for PDF, Pandoc writes Typst source and Typst typesets it into a pdf. One command, quarto render, runs all three steps."}

The split matters in practice. A failure in step 1 is a failure of *your code*: a missing
package, a wrong column name, a cell that raises an error. A failure in step 2 or 3 is a
failure of *the document*: a malformed table, an image too large for the page, a
format-specific option that does not exist. When a render fails, the error message tells
you which step stopped, and that tells you where to look.

::: think
A render of `london.qmd` stops with `KeyError: 'visits_2025'`. Which step failed, and where do
you look first?

Step 1, execute. A code cell asked the data for a column it does not have, so compare the cell
with the column names in the data file. The format settings are not the problem: Pandoc and
Typst never ran.
:::

<!-- Messages as Quarto 1.10.20 printed them, 2026-11-24: the moved cell of 05-compute.qmd, a
missing image, the format:html of first-report.qmd. -->

::: tryit
Three renders stopped. For each message, name the step it came from, or say that no step ran.

1. `NameError: name 'attractions' is not defined`
2. `[typst]: Compiling london.typ to london.pdf...error: file not found`
3. `ERROR: YAMLException: can not read a block mapping entry`

::: done
you have named a step, or none, for each, and can say whether to look at the code or at the
document.
:::
:::

**Answers.** The first is step 1: a cell used a name that no earlier cell had made, so look at
the code. The second is step 3: Typst could not find an image the page names, so look at the
document. The third is the trick: no step ran, because Quarto could not read the settings,
which it reads first.

::: why
Pandoc converts between many formats by reading every input into one internal document
model and writing every output from that model. That is why one Markdown file can become
both a Word document and a slide deck: neither output is derived from the other, so a heading
is a heading everywhere.
:::

### What comes out

Quarto's official list of formats is long and grouped by kind. This book uses two of the
kinds:

| Kind | Used in this book | Others |
|---|---|---|
| Documents | HTML, PDF (Typst), Word, EPUB | OpenDocument, PDF through LaTeX |
| Presentations | Reveal.js, PowerPoint | Beamer |

: Two kinds of output, as grouped in Quarto's official list. {#tbl-formats}

Quarto also writes Markdown dialects, wiki formats, Jupyter notebooks and more. Websites and
blogs are project types built from the same `.qmd` files; a dashboard is a format of its own,
whose headings lay out pages and rows (@sec-audiences).

## Quarto is not AI {#sec-not-ai}

This book pairs Quarto with a coding agent, and the pairing invites a misunderstanding:
that Quarto itself is an AI tool. It is not. Quarto is conventional software: given the same
source files and data, it writes the same outputs every time. It generates no text, code or
figures of its own, and sends nothing to an AI service.

The agent is a separate program. It reads and writes the files in your project folder
and runs commands you approve; Quarto then turns those files into formats. The two have
different failure modes, and the workflow in this book is designed around the difference:

| | Coding agent | Quarto |
|---|---|---|
| Output for the same input | varies from run to run | identical |
| Typical mistake | plausible but wrong code or prose | a precise, reproducible error |
| How you check it | read its changes, run them, compare with the data | read the rendered output |

: Two tools with different failure modes. {#tbl-split}

Because generation and rendering are separate, every mistake the agent makes lands in
a file you can read or a command you approve before anything is published: that gap is
where the *Check* step of the loop happens. And because the render is repeatable, anyone can
rebuild your outputs to confirm them, without trusting the agent at all.

::: think
Asked twice for the same chart, the agent writes two different code cells. If you keep
one and render it twice, do you get two different charts?

No. The agent varies; Quarto does not. Once the cell is in the file, every render runs the
same code on the same data, so you check the cell once and every rebuild inherits that check.
:::

::: pitfall
Quarto runs whatever code your cells contain. If a cell calls an AI service, the document
becomes as unpredictable as that service, and the cause is your code, not Quarto. Keep
calls to models out of rendered documents unless the variation is the point.
:::

## Reproducible: same source, same result {#sec-reproducible}

*Reproducible* is used loosely, so here is the precise sense this book means: someone else,
or you in six months, can rebuild the same results from the same files with one command,
and can see where every number came from. Four properties make that possible:

::: cards
One source
:   Text, code and data live in plain files in one folder. Nothing important exists only
    inside an application.

Numbers are computed
:   Every figure, table and number in a sentence comes from a code cell or inline code that
    reads the data. Nothing is typed in or pasted from elsewhere.

One command
:   `quarto render` rebuilds everything. There is no sequence of manual export steps to
    remember.

Versioned
:   Git, the version-control tool installed in @sec-setup, is something like Word's Track
    Changes for a whole folder, with a lasting history; a folder with its history is a
    *repository*. Each state you choose to record is a *commit*, with a message saying why.
:::

With Git, any earlier state can be restored, two states can be compared, and a result can be
tied to the exact files that made it. The project's Python packages are pinned too, in a
lockfile (`uv.lock`, introduced in @sec-environments), so a colleague's machine builds the same
*environment*, the Python version and packages the code runs with, as yours.

The promise has conditions: the same result comes from the same *inputs*, the same declared
environment and the same settings. Three things quietly break it:

- **Live data.** Data read from a website can change between two renders, so a project keeps
  a dated copy of its data in its folder.
- **An unfixed random seed.** Anything random, such as the starting points of a clustering method,
  repeats only when its *seed*, the number that starts the random sequence, is fixed.
- **A cache.** Quarto can keep computed results to save time (`freeze`). A frozen page runs
  again when its source changes, not when its data do, so it can serve an old result;
  @sec-publish-many shows how to clear it safely.

```{python}
#| label: ch1-first-rows
# Rows in the first report's data.
import csv

with open("../starters/first-report/data/visits.csv", newline="") as f:
    n_first_rows = sum(1 for _ in csv.DictReader(f))
```

Together these turn the drift problem around: correct one value in the data and render, and
every table, chart and sentence that quotes it updates, in every format. @sec-first-change has
you do exactly that, on a `{python} in_words(n_first_rows)`-row file.

::: think
You correct one number in the data. What do you retype in the report?

Nothing. You fix the data file and render again. If the answer is anything else, some
number in the report was typed rather than computed, and that is the bug to fix.
:::

::: pitfall
Reproducible does not mean correct. A wrong analysis reproduces perfectly: the same wrong
number appears in every format, every time. Reproducibility makes errors *findable*,
because anyone can trace a number back to its code and data, but you still have to check
results against their sources. @sec-causation is an extended example of a result that
reproduces cleanly and still must not be read the way it first appears.
:::

## When Quarto is the wrong tool {#sec-wrong-tool}

Quarto earns its keep when the same content is rebuilt, either because the data change or
because the content goes to several audiences. It costs you a plain-text workflow, a
command line and some setup. That trade is not always worth making:

- **Collaborators who edit in Word.** If the people who revise the document work with
  tracked changes, they can comment on the Word output, but their edits have to be carried
  back into the source by hand. For multi-author line editing, a shared word processor may
  simply fit better.
- **Designed layouts.** Quarto produces structured documents: headings, paragraphs,
  figures, tables. Typst and CSS can take the look a long way, but a poster or a
  brand-heavy brochure laid out to the millimetre is easier in a design tool.
- **Format fidelity at the edges.** Each format can only carry what it supports: in
  Quarto's PowerPoint output a table cannot hold pictures, so the London guide's photo table shows each photo's
  alt text in its `pptx` version instead. Check every format you promise to deliver.
- **One-off documents.** A two-paragraph note with no data and no second audience gains
  little from a build system.
- **Design and co-editing in a start-up.** A designed pitch deck, a marketing site and a plan
  the co-founders comment on in Google Docs or Notion can stay in those tools. The method pays
  where a start-up's numbers change, as in the monthly investor update
  (@sec-at-work-startup has the full case).

::: practice
A useful test: will this document be built a second time? If the data will change, if a
second audience will need it in another format, or if someone will ask "where did this
number come from?", the plain-text workflow pays for itself quickly. If none of these is
likely, use whatever is fastest.
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: keyideas
- Reports drift when their outputs are edited by hand; editing one source and letting a
  program rebuild every output removes the copies.
- `quarto render` executes the cells, converts with Pandoc and, for PDF, typesets with Typst;
  the step that stops tells you where to look.
- Quarto is not AI: the same source and data give the same outputs. Check the agent's work
  once; anyone can rebuild yours without trusting it.
- Reproducible means one source, computed numbers, one command and versioned files. It earns
  trust and makes errors findable, not absent.
- Live data, an unfixed seed and a cache break the promise quietly: a frozen page re-runs when
  its source changes, not its data.
- Quarto pays for documents built again, such as monthly reports and investor updates; it is
  the wrong tool for co-editing, designed layouts and one-off notes.
:::

Quarto, though, renders only what it is given. In this book a coding agent writes those
sources, and its output varies from run to run and can be confidently wrong. How do you ask
such a program for work, and how do you check what comes back before anything is published?
@sec-assistant answers.
